subject: HSS
title: American Government & Civics (S1) / Economics (S2)
description: Semester 1 (Principles of American Democracy) examines the philosophical foundations of the Constitution, rights and responsibilities, the three branches, landmark Supreme Court cases, elections, federalism with a focus on California state and local government, the media, comparative systems, and a civic action project. Semester 2 (Economics) covers scarcity and economic systems, supply and demand, market structures, the role of government, labor markets, macroeconomic indicators, fiscal and monetary policy, and international trade. Primary sources (Federalist Papers, court opinions, ballot measures, Fed statements, BLS data) anchor every week.
framework: California History–Social Science Content Standards, Grade 12 (Principles of American Democracy and Economics); 2016 California History–Social Science Framework. Government codes are prefixed GOV-12.x and economics codes ECON-12.x.

standards.GOV-12.1: Explain the fundamental principles and moral values of American democracy as expressed in the Constitution and other founding documents.
standards.GOV-12.1.1: Analyze the influence of ancient Greek, Roman, English, and leading European political thinkers (Locke, Montesquieu, etc.) on the development of American government.
standards.GOV-12.1.2: Discuss the character of American democracy and its promise and perils as articulated by Alexis de Tocqueville.
standards.GOV-12.1.4: Explain how the Constitution balances the classical republican concern for the public good with the classical liberal concern for individual rights, and how the Declaration and Constitution join liberal constitutionalism and democracy.
standards.GOV-12.1.5: Describe separated and shared powers, the role of organized interests (Federalist 10), checks and balances (Federalist 51), an independent judiciary (Federalist 78), enumerated powers, rule of law, federalism, and civilian control of the military.
standards.GOV-12.1.6: Understand that the Bill of Rights limits the powers of the federal government and state governments.
standards.GOV-12.2: Evaluate and take and defend positions on the scope and limits of rights and obligations as democratic citizens.
standards.GOV-12.2.1: Discuss the meaning and importance of each of the rights guaranteed under the Bill of Rights and how each is secured.
standards.GOV-12.2.2: Explain how economic rights are secured and their importance to the individual and society.
standards.GOV-12.2.4: Understand the obligations of civic-mindedness, including voting, jury duty, military service, and community service.
standards.GOV-12.2.5: Describe the reciprocity between rights and obligations; why enjoyment of one's rights entails respect for the rights of others.
standards.GOV-12.3: Evaluate and take and defend positions on what the fundamental values and principles of civil society are, their interdependence, and the meaning and importance of those values and principles for a free society.
standards.GOV-12.3.1: Explain how civil society provides opportunities for individuals to associate for social, cultural, religious, economic, and political purposes.
standards.GOV-12.3.2: Explain how civil society makes it possible for people, individually or in association with others, to bring their influence to bear on government.
standards.GOV-12.4: Analyze the unique roles and responsibilities of the three branches of government as established by the U.S. Constitution.
standards.GOV-12.4.1: Discuss Article I of the Constitution as it relates to the legislative branch, including eligibility, terms, election, and powers of Congress.
standards.GOV-12.4.2: Explain the process through which the Constitution can be amended.
standards.GOV-12.4.3: Identify their current representatives in the legislative branch of the national government.
standards.GOV-12.4.4: Discuss Article II of the Constitution as it relates to the executive branch, including eligibility, terms, election, and powers of the president.
standards.GOV-12.4.5: Discuss Article III of the Constitution as it relates to judicial power, including the length of terms of judges and the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.
standards.GOV-12.4.6: Explain the processes of selection and confirmation of Supreme Court justices.
standards.GOV-12.5: Summarize landmark U.S. Supreme Court interpretations of the Constitution and its amendments.
standards.GOV-12.5.1: Understand the changing interpretations of the Bill of Rights over time, including interpretations of basic freedoms (religion, speech, press, petition, assembly) in court cases.
standards.GOV-12.5.2: Analyze judicial activism and judicial restraint and the effects of each policy over the decades.
standards.GOV-12.5.3: Evaluate the effects of the Court's interpretations of the Constitution in Marbury v. Madison, McCulloch v. Maryland, and United States v. Nixon, with emphasis on checks and balances.
standards.GOV-12.5.4: Explain the controversies that have resulted over changing interpretations of civil rights, including Plessy v. Ferguson, Brown v. Board of Education, Miranda v. Arizona, Regents of the University of California v. Bakke, and United States v. Virginia (VMI).
standards.GOV-12.6: Evaluate issues regarding campaigns for national, state, and local elective offices.
standards.GOV-12.6.1: Analyze the origin, development, and role of political parties.
standards.GOV-12.6.2: Discuss the history of the nomination process for presidential candidates and the increasing importance of primaries.
standards.GOV-12.6.3: Evaluate the roles of polls, campaign advertising, and controversies over campaign funding.
standards.GOV-12.6.4: Describe the means that citizens use to participate in the political process (voting, campaigning, lobbying, filing a legal challenge, demonstrating, petitioning, picketing, running for office).
standards.GOV-12.6.5: Discuss the features of direct democracy in numerous states (e.g., initiatives, referendums, recall).
standards.GOV-12.6.6: Analyze trends in voter turnout; causes and effects of reapportionment and redistricting, with special attention to spatial districting and the rights of minorities; and the function of the Electoral College.
standards.GOV-12.7: Analyze and compare the powers and procedures of the national, state, tribal, and local governments.
standards.GOV-12.7.1: Explain how conflicts between levels of government and branches of government are resolved.
standards.GOV-12.7.2: Identify the major responsibilities and sources of revenue for state and local governments.
standards.GOV-12.7.3: Discuss reserved powers and concurrent powers of state governments.
standards.GOV-12.7.4: Discuss the Ninth and Tenth Amendments and interpretations of the extent of the federal government's power.
standards.GOV-12.7.5: Explain how public policy is formed, including the setting of the public agenda and implementation of it through regulations and executive orders.
standards.GOV-12.7.6: Compare the processes of lawmaking at each of the three levels of government, including the role of lobbying and the media.
standards.GOV-12.7.7: Identify the organization and jurisdiction of federal, state, and local (e.g., California) courts and the interrelationships among them.
standards.GOV-12.7.8: Understand the scope of presidential power and decision making through examination of case studies.
standards.GOV-12.8: Evaluate and take and defend positions on the influence of the media on American political life.
standards.GOV-12.8.1: Discuss the meaning and importance of a free and responsible press.
standards.GOV-12.8.2: Describe the roles of broadcast, print, and electronic media, including the Internet, as means of communication in American politics.
standards.GOV-12.8.3: Explain how public officials use the media to communicate with the citizenry and to shape public opinion.
standards.GOV-12.9: Analyze the origins, characteristics, and development of different political systems across time, with emphasis on the quest for political democracy, its advances, and its obstacles.
standards.GOV-12.9.3: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of federal, confederal, and unitary systems of government.
standards.GOV-12.9.4: Describe for at least two countries the consequences of conditions that gave rise to tyrannies during certain periods.
standards.GOV-12.9.5: Identify the forms of illegitimate power that twentieth-century African, Asian, and Latin American dictators used to gain and hold office and the conditions and interests that supported them.
standards.GOV-12.9.6: Identify the ideologies, causes, stages, and outcomes of major Mexican, Central American, and South American revolutions in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
standards.GOV-12.9.7: Identify the successes of relatively new democracies in Africa, Asia, and Latin America and the ideas, leaders, and general societal conditions that have launched and sustained, or failed to sustain, them.
standards.GOV-12.10: Formulate questions about and defend their analyses of tensions within our constitutional democracy and the importance of maintaining a balance between majority rule and individual rights, liberty and equality, state and national authority, and other enduring tensions.
standards.ECON-12.1: Understand common economic terms and concepts and economic reasoning.
standards.ECON-12.1.1: Examine the causal relationship between scarcity and the need for choices.
standards.ECON-12.1.2: Explain opportunity cost and marginal benefit and marginal cost.
standards.ECON-12.1.3: Identify the difference between monetary and nonmonetary incentives and how changes in incentives cause changes in behavior.
standards.ECON-12.1.4: Evaluate the role of private property as an incentive in conserving and improving scarce resources, including renewable and nonrenewable natural resources.
standards.ECON-12.2: Analyze the elements of America's market economy in a global setting.
standards.ECON-12.2.1: Understand the relationship of the concept of incentives to the law of supply and the relationship of the concept of incentives and substitutes to the law of demand.
standards.ECON-12.2.2: Discuss the effects of changes in supply and/or demand on the relative scarcity, price, and quantity of particular products.
standards.ECON-12.2.3: Explain the roles of property rights, competition, and profit in a market economy.
standards.ECON-12.2.4: Explain how prices reflect the relative scarcity of goods and services and perform the allocative function in a market economy.
standards.ECON-12.2.5: Understand the process by which competition among buyers and sellers determines a market price.
standards.ECON-12.2.6: Describe the effect of price controls on buyers and sellers.
standards.ECON-12.2.7: Analyze how domestic and international competition in a market economy affects goods and services produced and the quality, quantity, and price of those products.
standards.ECON-12.2.8: Explain the role of profit as the incentive to entrepreneurs in a market economy.
standards.ECON-12.2.9: Describe the functions of the financial markets.
standards.ECON-12.2.10: Discuss the economic principles that guide the location of agricultural production and industry and the spatial distribution of transportation and retail facilities.
standards.ECON-12.3: Analyze the influence of the federal government on the American economy.
standards.ECON-12.3.1: Understand how the role of government in a market economy often includes providing for national defense, addressing environmental concerns, defining and enforcing property rights, attempting to make markets more competitive, and protecting consumers' rights.
standards.ECON-12.3.2: Identify the factors that may cause the costs of government actions to outweigh the benefits.
standards.ECON-12.3.3: Describe the aims of government fiscal policies (taxation, borrowing, spending) and their influence on production, employment, and price levels.
standards.ECON-12.3.4: Understand the aims and tools of monetary policy and their influence on economic activity (the Federal Reserve).
standards.ECON-12.4: Analyze the elements of the U.S. labor market in a global setting.
standards.ECON-12.4.1: Understand the operations of the labor market, including the circumstances surrounding the establishment of principal American labor unions, procedures that unions use to gain benefits for their members, the effects of unionization, the minimum wage, and unemployment insurance.
standards.ECON-12.4.2: Describe the current economy and labor market, including the types of goods and services produced, the types of skills workers need, the effects of rapid technological change, and the impact of international competition.
standards.ECON-12.4.3: Discuss wage differences among jobs and professions, using the laws of demand and supply and the concept of productivity.
standards.ECON-12.4.4: Explain the effects of international mobility of capital and labor on the U.S. economy.
standards.ECON-12.5: Analyze the aggregate economic behavior of the U.S. economy.
standards.ECON-12.5.1: Distinguish between nominal and real data.
standards.ECON-12.5.2: Define, calculate, and explain the significance of an unemployment rate, the number of new jobs created monthly, an inflation or deflation rate, and a rate of economic growth.
standards.ECON-12.5.3: Distinguish between short-term and long-term interest rates and explain their relative significance.
standards.ECON-12.6: Analyze issues of international trade and explain how the U.S. economy affects, and is affected by, economic forces beyond the United States's borders.
standards.ECON-12.6.1: Identify the gains in consumption and production efficiency from trade, with emphasis on the main products and changing geographic patterns of twentieth-century trade among countries in the Western Hemisphere.
standards.ECON-12.6.2: Compare the reasons for and the effects of trade restrictions during the Great Depression compared with present-day arguments among labor, business, and political leaders over the effects of free trade on the economic and social interests of various groups of Americans.
standards.ECON-12.6.3: Understand the changing role of international political borders and territorial sovereignty in a global economy.
standards.ECON-12.6.4: Explain foreign exchange, the manner in which exchange rates are determined, and the effects of the dollar's gaining (or losing) value relative to other currencies.

units.title: Foundations of American Democracy
units.big_idea: The Constitution blends ancient, English, and Enlightenment ideas to limit power and protect liberty.

units.title: Rights, Responsibilities, and Civil Society
units.big_idea: Rights depend on citizens who respect others' rights and participate in civil society.

units.title: The Three Branches
units.big_idea: Separated and shared powers force the branches to cooperate and check one another.

units.title: The Supreme Court and Landmark Cases
units.big_idea: The Court's interpretations of the Constitution change over time and reshape American life.

units.title: Elections, Parties, and Participation
units.big_idea: Citizens influence government through parties, campaigns, voting, and direct democracy.

units.title: Federalism: California State, Local, and Tribal Government
units.big_idea: Power is shared among national, state, tribal, and local governments, and most daily services are local.

units.title: Media, Comparative Government, and Civic Action
units.big_idea: A free press, comparison with other systems, and informed action keep democracy healthy.

units.title: Economic Fundamentals
units.big_idea: Scarcity forces choices, and every choice has an opportunity cost.

units.title: Markets: Supply, Demand, and Competition
units.big_idea: Prices coordinate millions of decisions by signaling relative scarcity.

units.title: Government and the Economy
units.big_idea: Government corrects some market failures, but its actions also have costs.

units.title: Labor Markets
units.big_idea: Wages reflect supply, demand, and productivity in a changing global labor market.

units.title: Macroeconomics, Money, and the Fed
units.big_idea: GDP, unemployment, and inflation measure the economy's health, and fiscal and monetary policy try to stabilize it.

units.title: International Economics
units.big_idea: Trade raises total output through specialization but creates winners and losers.

units.title: Economics Capstone
units.big_idea: Economic reasoning helps citizens evaluate real policy choices.

objectives: Trace Greek, Roman, English, and Enlightenment influences

days.title: Why government?
days.work: Read Hobbes and Locke excerpts on the state of nature and write a paragraph comparing their views on why people form governments.

days.title: Ancient roots
days.work: Compare Athenian direct democracy and the Roman Republic; chart which features the Framers adopted or rejected.

days.title: English roots
days.work: Read excerpts of Magna Carta (1215) and the English Bill of Rights (1689); highlight limits on the monarch that reappear in the Constitution.

days.title: The Declaration
days.work: Annotate the Declaration's second paragraph, identifying Locke's ideas, and categorize the grievances by type.

days.title: Check
days.work: Take a quiz and write a 300-word response: which thinker most influenced the founding, with evidence?

weeks.topic: The Constitution and the Federalist Papers

days.title: Articles to Constitution
days.work: List weaknesses of the Articles of Confederation and match each to a fix in the Constitution.

days.title: Federalist 10
days.work: Read Federalist 10 and explain Madison's argument that a large republic controls the effects of faction.

days.title: Federalist 51 and 78
days.work: Read excerpts of Federalist 51 ('ambition must be made to counteract ambition') and 78 (independent judiciary); diagram checks and balances.

days.title: Anti-Federalists and Tocqueville
days.work: Read Brutus No. 1 and a Tocqueville excerpt on 'tyranny of the majority'; explain how the Bill of Rights answered these fears.

days.title: Unit 1 test
days.work: Take the Unit 1 test with a DBQ-style essay on how the Constitution limits government power.

objectives: Explain the protections in each amendment

days.title: The First Amendment
days.work: Read the First Amendment and classify 10 scenarios (school speech, protest permits, religious displays) as protected or not.

days.title: Amendments 2–8
days.work: Create a chart of Amendments 2–8 with a modern example for each, focusing on rights of the accused.

days.title: Incorporation
days.work: Read about the 14th Amendment's due process clause and incorporation; explain how the Bill of Rights came to limit states.

days.title: Economic rights
days.work: Discuss economic rights (property, contracts, choosing an occupation, the Takings Clause) and analyze Kelo v. New London's eminent domain ruling.

days.title: Rights game & check
days.work: Play iCivics 'Do I Have a Right?' and take a Bill of Rights quiz.

objectives: Explain how civil society influences government

days.title: Citizenship
days.work: Take the USCIS 100-question naturalization civics test and research how people become U.S. citizens.

days.title: Obligations
days.work: Research jury duty in California (eligibility, process) and Selective Service registration; write about why each matters.

days.title: Civil society
days.work: Read Tocqueville on Americans' associations; map 10 civic organizations in your community and their purposes.

days.title: Interview
days.work: Interview a volunteer or nonprofit leader about how their group influences public decisions.

days.title: Unit 2 check
days.work: Take the Unit 2 test with a position essay on the balance between rights and responsibilities.

objectives: Describe Article I powers and structure

days.title: Article I
days.work: Read Article I and chart qualifications, terms, and unique powers of the House and Senate.

days.title: Your representatives
days.work: Look up your U.S. Representative and both U.S. Senators; summarize their committees and one recent vote each.

days.title: Powers of Congress
days.work: Sort Article I, Section 8 powers into categories (money, commerce, defense) and discuss the elastic clause.

days.title: Committees and leadership
days.work: Diagram congressional leadership (Speaker, majority leaders, whips) and the committee system.

days.title: Check
days.work: Take a quiz on Congress's structure and powers.

weeks.topic: How a bill becomes law; amending the Constitution

days.title: Lawmaking
days.work: Flowchart how a bill becomes law, including committees, floor votes, conference, and veto override.

days.title: Track a bill
days.work: Use congress.gov to track one current bill and record its sponsor, committee, and status.

days.title: Mock legislature
days.work: Write a short bill, 'mark it up' with family as a committee, and simulate a floor vote with amendments.

days.title: Amendments
days.work: Read Article V; compare successful (19th, 26th) and failed (ERA) amendments and explain why some fail.

days.title: Check
days.work: Write a 400-word reflection on why the founders made lawmaking slow; take a short quiz.

materials: Truman's Korean War / Kennedy's Cuban Missile Crisis documents (DocsTeach)

days.title: Article II
days.work: Read Article II and list formal powers; compare to informal powers like 'bully pulpit.'

days.title: Executive orders
days.work: Read a recent executive order from the Federal Register and analyze its legal basis and limits.

days.title: Bureaucracy
days.work: Diagram the 15 executive departments and research one independent agency (EPA, FCC) and what it regulates.

days.title: Case study
days.work: Analyze primary sources from the Cuban Missile Crisis and evaluate Kennedy's decision-making options.

days.title: Check
days.work: Take a quiz and play iCivics 'Executive Command.'

weeks.assessment: Executive branch quiz and case-study analysis.

objectives: Describe Article III and the federal court system

days.title: Article III
days.work: Read Article III; diagram district courts, circuit courts, and the Supreme Court; locate California in the Ninth Circuit.

days.title: How cases reach the Court
days.work: Learn the certiorari process and the 'rule of four'; analyze how few petitions are granted.

days.title: Selecting justices
days.work: Watch a segment of a recent confirmation hearing and evaluate the questions senators asked.

days.title: Reading an opinion
days.work: Read the syllabus of a recent Supreme Court opinion and identify the question, holding, and reasoning.

days.title: Unit 3 test
days.work: Take the Unit 3 test on the three branches.

objectives: Evaluate Marbury, McCulloch, and U.S. v. Nixon

days.title: Marbury v. Madison
days.work: Read excerpts of Marshall's opinion and explain how the Court established judicial review.

days.title: McCulloch v. Maryland
days.work: Analyze 'the power to tax involves the power to destroy' and how McCulloch expanded federal power.

days.title: U.S. v. Nixon
days.work: Listen to Oyez audio excerpts and explain how the case limited executive privilege.

days.title: Activism vs. restraint
days.work: Read short essays on judicial philosophy (originalism, living constitution) and apply each to one case.

days.title: Check
days.work: Write a 500-word analysis of how one case strengthened checks and balances.

weeks.topic: Civil rights and civil liberties cases
objectives: Trace changing interpretations of civil rights

days.title: Plessy to Brown
days.work: Compare excerpts from Plessy v. Ferguson (including Harlan's dissent) and Brown v. Board; explain the reversal.

days.title: Student rights
days.work: Analyze Tinker v. Des Moines and a later student speech case; discuss limits on student speech.

days.title: Rights of the accused
days.work: Analyze Miranda v. Arizona and Gideon v. Wainwright and their effect on policing and courts.

days.title: California cases
days.work: Analyze Regents of UC v. Bakke and California's Proposition 209 and how admissions policy changed.

days.title: Moot court
days.work: Prepare and argue one side of a landmark case for 5 minutes before a family 'bench'; take the Unit 4 test.

weeks.assessment: Moot court argument and Unit 4 test.

objectives: Analyze the role of political parties

days.title: Origin of parties
days.work: Read Washington's warning about factions in his Farewell Address and trace the development of the two-party system.

days.title: Nominations
days.work: Explain how presidential primaries and conventions evolved and how California's top-two primary works.

days.title: Campaign ads
days.work: Analyze three historical campaign ads for persuasive techniques and target audiences.

days.title: Money in politics
days.work: Use FEC.gov to compare fundraising for two candidates and analyze Citizens United v. FEC.

days.title: Polls
days.work: Evaluate two recent polls for sample size, margin of error, and question wording; take a quiz.

weeks.topic: Voting, direct democracy, and the Electoral College
objectives: Analyze California ballot measures and the Electoral College

days.title: Register
days.work: Learn California's voter pre-registration at 16–17 and registration at 18; complete or walk through the registertovote.ca.gov process.

days.title: Ballot measures
days.work: Read a recent California ballot proposition in the Official Voter Guide, including LAO analysis and pro/con arguments, and decide how you would vote.

days.title: Recall and referendum
days.work: Compare the 2003 and 2021 gubernatorial recall elections and the process for qualifying measures.

days.title: Redistricting
days.work: Explore maps from California's Citizens Redistricting Commission and explain how gerrymandering works.

days.title: Electoral College
days.work: Calculate electoral votes for a sample election and debate keeping vs. abolishing the Electoral College; take the Unit 5 test.

objectives: Distinguish delegated, reserved, and concurrent powers

days.title: Dividing power
days.work: Create a Venn diagram of federal, state, and concurrent powers and discuss the 9th and 10th Amendments.

days.title: Federal-state conflict
days.work: Analyze a federal-state conflict (cannabis law, vehicle emissions waivers, immigration) and how courts resolved it.

days.title: California's government
days.work: Compare the California Constitution with the U.S. Constitution (length, amendment process, Declaration of Rights).

days.title: State lawmaking
days.work: Track a bill in the California Legislature on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and compare the process with Congress.

days.title: Check
days.work: Take a quiz on federalism and California government.

weeks.topic: Local and tribal government, budgets, and courts
objectives: Identify local government responsibilities and revenue

days.title: Local government
days.work: Map who provides your water, schools, police, fire, roads, and parks (city, county, special district).

days.title: Budgets
days.work: Analyze your city or county budget: identify the top revenue sources and top spending categories; explain Proposition 13's effect.

days.title: Tribal governments
days.work: Research a California tribal government's structure and its government-to-government relationship with the state.

days.title: California courts
days.work: Diagram superior courts, courts of appeal, and the California Supreme Court; compare to federal courts.

days.title: Attend a meeting
days.work: Attend or watch a recorded city council or school board meeting; write a summary and a public comment you could give. Take the Unit 6 test.

objectives: Explain the role of a free press
materials: New York Times v. United States (Pentagon Papers) summary
two news sources on the same story

days.title: Free press
days.work: Analyze the Pentagon Papers case (New York Times v. U.S.) and explain prior restraint.

days.title: Comparing coverage
days.work: Compare coverage of the same political story in three outlets and identify framing and word-choice differences.

days.title: Lateral reading
days.work: Practice lateral reading to fact-check five viral social-media claims.

days.title: Officials and media
days.work: Analyze how a public official uses social media to shape opinion; compare to FDR's fireside chats.

days.title: Check
days.work: Write a media-literacy guide for voters and take a short quiz.

objectives: Analyze the rise of tyrannies and new democracies
materials: Mandela 'I Am Prepared to Die' speech excerpt

days.title: System types
days.work: Compare federal, confederal, and unitary systems and presidential vs. parliamentary democracy (U.S. vs. UK).

days.title: Rise of tyranny
days.work: Analyze conditions that gave rise to dictatorship in Germany (1933) and one Latin American case (e.g., Chile 1973).

days.title: Revolutions
days.work: Analyze the causes and outcomes of the Mexican Revolution (1910) and its constitution of 1917.

days.title: New democracies
days.work: Read Mandela's 'I Am Prepared to Die' excerpt and analyze South Africa's democratic transition; compare one other new democracy.

days.title: Check
days.work: Write a comparison of two countries using Freedom House scores and take a quiz.

weeks.topic: Enduring tensions and civic action project
objectives: Analyze enduring tensions in constitutional democracy

days.title: Enduring tensions
days.work: Read excerpts of King's 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' and identify tensions between law, order, liberty, and equality.

days.title: Choose an issue
days.work: Choose a local or state issue, research multiple perspectives, and identify the decision-makers.

days.title: Plan action
days.work: Plan one civic action (letter to a legislator, public comment, petition, volunteer project) with a timeline.

days.title: Take action
days.work: Carry out the action: send the letter, deliver public comment, or complete the volunteer hours, and document it.

days.title: Reflect
days.work: Write a reflection on what you learned about how change happens in a democracy.

days.title: Review: foundations & rights
days.work: Create a one-page study guide on founding principles and the Bill of Rights.

days.title: Review: branches & courts
days.work: Complete a review set matching powers to branches and cases to holdings.

days.title: Civic action presentation
days.work: Present your civic action project in 5 minutes.

days.title: Practice exam
days.work: Retake the USCIS civics test and complete a practice exam.

days.title: Semester final
days.work: Take the Government semester final with a DBQ essay on an enduring constitutional tension.

days.title: Scarcity
days.work: List 10 scarce resources in your life (time, money, space) and identify a choice each forces.

days.title: Opportunity cost
days.work: Calculate the opportunity cost of attending college vs. working full-time for four years.

days.title: PPF
days.work: Graph a production possibilities frontier for a household (meals vs. cleaning) and identify efficient, inefficient, and unattainable points.

days.title: Marginal thinking
days.work: Use a marginal benefit/marginal cost table (slices of pizza, hours of study) to find the optimal choice.

days.title: Check
days.work: Take a quiz on scarcity, PPF, and marginal analysis.

objectives: Compare market, command, and mixed economies
materials: Adam Smith, Wealth of Nations excerpt (Project Gutenberg)

days.title: Incentives
days.work: Classify 10 incentives (bottle deposits, grades, fines, praise) as monetary or nonmonetary and predict behavior changes.

days.title: Adam Smith
days.work: Read the 'invisible hand' and pin-factory excerpts from The Wealth of Nations and summarize Smith's argument.

days.title: Command economies
days.work: Compare East and West Germany or North and South Korea using GDP-per-capita data.

days.title: Property and conservation
days.work: Analyze how property rights affect conservation (e.g., California groundwater rights, fishing quotas).

days.title: Unit 8 test
